description: Specificity, overload, progression, reversibility and the FITT principle applied to training programmes.
content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Elite athletes do not train randomly. Their programmes are built on scientific principles that ensure each session causes the right adaptations without injury or wasted effort. Two frameworks summarise these principles: SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery) and FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type). Together they provide a blueprint for designing any training programme, from a beginner’s fitness plan to an international athlete’s competition preparation.

SPOR: The Four Principles

Specificity — training must be designed to match the specific demands of the sport and the individual. A sprinter must train the fast-twitch muscle fibres and anaerobic energy systems used in a 100 m race; continuous low-intensity jogging would not develop the right adaptations. A swimmer should train in the water to develop sport-specific cardiovascular and muscular endurance rather than only running. If the training is not specific to the sport, the gains will not transfer to performance.

Progressive overload — the body adapts to the demands placed upon it. Once it has adapted, the same training stimulus produces no further improvement. To keep progressing, the training load must be gradually and continuously increased — using the FITT variables. A weight trainer who always lifts the same weight will plateau; they must add weight, more sets or more repetitions to continue building strength. The progression must be gradual: too-rapid increases lead to injury.

Reversibility — fitness adaptations are not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced — due to injury, illness or a long break — the body returns towards its pre-training state. Cardiovascular adaptations (such as a lower resting heart rate and larger stroke volume) reverse relatively quickly, often within a few weeks. Muscle mass is lost more slowly. This principle underlines why consistent, year-round training is more effective than intense bursts followed by long rest periods.

Recovery — sufficient rest must be built into any training programme. Without recovery time, the body cannot repair the microscopic muscle damage caused by training and cannot make the physiological adaptations that lead to improved fitness. Overtraining — training too hard without enough rest — leads to fatigue, declining performance and increased injury risk. Planning rest days or lower-intensity recovery sessions between hard efforts is as important as the training itself.

Key Fact

SPOR: Specificity (match training to sport demands), Progressive Overload (gradually increase load to keep adapting), Overload/reversibility (gains are lost if training stops — see Reversibility), Recovery (adequate rest allows the body to adapt). Note: OCR uses SPOR — Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery — not SPORT. There is no Tedium principle in OCR.

SPOR and FITT are complementary but distinct. SPOR gives the overarching principles — the “why” and “what” of training design (should training be specific? yes; should load progress? yes; must recovery be planned? yes). FITT gives the four variables you can actually manipulate to achieve those principles — the “how.” For example, applying progressive overload (a SPOR principle) is achieved by increasing frequency, intensity or time (all FITT variables). Understanding this relationship is often tested through questions asking you to “apply the FITT principles to achieve progressive overload for a specific athlete.”

FITT: The Four Training Variables

Frequency — how often a person trains per week. A beginner might train twice a week to allow full recovery; an elite endurance athlete may train twice a day. Frequency must be balanced against recovery: too many sessions without rest leads to overtraining and injury, too few limits adaptation.

Intensity — how hard the training is. Intensity can be expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate (for cardiovascular training), a percentage of one rep max (for weight training), or by effort level or speed. The aerobic training zone is 60–80% of maximum heart rate; the anaerobic zone is 80–90%. Choosing the right intensity ensures the correct energy system is stressed.

Time — the duration of a training session or individual exercise bout. A continuous run lasting 30 minutes will primarily stress the aerobic system; interval sprint sessions of 10 seconds each stress the anaerobic system.

Type — the method of training used. Type must align with the principle of specificity: a long-distance runner should use continuous training; a boxer should use circuit training with punching drills and HIIT; a gymnast needing flexibility should include stretching within a structured warm-up and cool-down. Choosing the wrong type of training may improve a general component of fitness without translating to sport-specific performance gains.

Key Fact

FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard — linked to training zones and heart rate %), Time (how long), Type (which training method). All four can be increased to apply progressive overload. Intensity links directly to training thresholds: aerobic 60–80% max HR; anaerobic 80–90% max HR.

A county-level 400 m freestyle swimmer applies the principles as follows. Specificity: all endurance sessions are in the pool using freestyle technique, not on a running track. Progressive overload: over 12 weeks the swimmer increases weekly distance by 10% and gradually shortens rest intervals between repetitions. Reversibility: during the off-season the swimmer maintains 50% of their training volume with twice-weekly pool sessions so that cardiovascular adaptations are not lost. Recovery: a complete rest day is built in after every two hard training days to allow muscle repair and adaptation. For FITT: frequency moves from 4 to 6 sessions per week over the training block; intensity is set at 70% of max HR for aerobic sets and 85% for higher-intensity sets; time per session increases from 60 to 90 minutes; type rotates between continuous, fartlek and interval training in the pool.

Applying SPOR and FITT Together

The most effective training programmes use both frameworks simultaneously. Specificity determines the training type; progressive overload is achieved by manipulating frequency, intensity and time over weeks and months; reversibility reminds the coach to maintain a training stimulus during breaks; and recovery ensures adequate rest is planned so the body can adapt. When you are asked to “design a training programme” or “evaluate the effectiveness of a training plan,” check whether all four SPOR principles and all four FITT variables are appropriately applied.
exam_tip_html: On an “8-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sporting example. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progressive overload” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: OCR uses SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery) — there is no Tedium principle. Confusing this with other boards’ acronyms is a common error.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SPOR stands for Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility and Recovery — these are the overarching principles that should underpin any training programme. OCR does not include Tedium.
  • FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type — these are the four variables that can be adjusted to implement progressive overload and ensure specificity.
  • SPOR and FITT work together: SPOR explains why changes should be made; FITT explains how to make them in practice.

practice_questions.text: Identify which letter of the SPOR acronym represents the idea that fitness gains can be lost when training stops.
Define the term 'progressive overload' as it applies to a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the training load must be increased; 1 mark for stating that this increase must be gradual (over time) so the body continues to adapt and improve (accept: the stimulus must increase because the body adapts to the current load and no longer improves without a new challenge).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the FITT principles can be applied to help a club-level tennis player improve their cardiovascular endurance during pre-season.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for applying any three of the four FITT variables to the scenario with specific detail. Frequency example: train 4 times a week rather than twice, as cardiovascular gains require more sessions (1). Intensity example: set sessions at 70–80% of maximum heart rate to work in the aerobic training zone (1). Time example: sessions of 45–60 minutes to ensure sustained aerobic demand (1). Type example: use continuous training (e.g. cycling, running) to develop cardiovascular endurance specifically (1). Each answer must include the variable name and a specific application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a coach can use the principle of specificity when designing a training programme for a 400 m track cyclist.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining specificity (training must match the demands of the sport/activity); 1 mark for explaining the specific energy system demands of 400 m track cycling (high-intensity anaerobic effort over approximately 40–50 seconds, with significant lactic acid production); 1 mark for explaining how training type should reflect this (interval training or HIIT on the bike, not long-distance continuous running); 1 mark for explaining how muscle specificity applies (training the quadriceps, gluteals and hip flexors through cycling-specific movements rather than gym exercises that do not replicate the cycling action).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level distance runner has been following the same 10 km running programme for three months with no improvement in race times. Analyse how the SPOR and FITT principles could be used to redesign the programme so that it leads to further performance improvements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies that the lack of improvement is explained by the principle of progressive overload — the body has adapted to the current stimulus; applies at least three FITT variables specifically (e.g. increase frequency from 3 to 5 sessions per week; increase intensity by introducing 80–85% max HR threshold runs; increase time of long runs by 10% per week); identifies specificity as supporting continued running-based sessions; raises reversibility to advise against abrupt rest periods; addresses recovery by recommending planned rest days; provides a coherent analysis of how these changes would lead to further cardiovascular and muscular endurance adaptation. Sporting context maintained throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): identifies progressive overload as the issue; applies two or more FITT variables with some specificity; some reference to sporting context.

Developing (2 marks): identifies that training needs to be harder or more varied; limited use of SPOR/FITT terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant principle mentioned with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A school sports coach is designing an annual training programme for a Year 11 football squad. Evaluate how effectively the SPOR principles can be applied to team sport training compared to individual sport training, considering both the benefits and the challenges for a football coach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): evaluates each SPOR principle with a two-sided argument. Specificity: in individual sports (e.g. marathon running) specificity is straightforward — one performer, one event; in football, specificity is harder because different positions require different fitness profiles (a goalkeeper needs different components from a midfielder), so a whole-squad programme may not be fully specific for every player. Progressive overload: easy to apply individually; harder in team training because players start from different fitness baselines — a blanket 10% increase in session intensity may overload some players while under-loading others. Reversibility: applies equally to both; coaches of both individual and team sport must plan for off-season maintenance. Recovery: in team sport, fixture schedules may not allow ideal recovery between matches, requiring careful management of training load in-season. Evaluates the overall effectiveness, naming specific football examples and contrasting with individual sport examples throughout. Balanced argument sustained.

Secure (5–6 marks): all four SPOR principles covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to football with some comparison to individual sport; generally accurate.

Developing (3–4 marks): at least two SPOR principles covered; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): basic reference to one or two principles with minimal analysis.

knowledge_checks.q: Which principle of training states that training must match the specific demands of the sport?
An athlete increases their weekly training sessions from three to five per week. Which FITT variable have they changed?
The principle that states fitness gains will be lost when training stops is called _____.
In the FITT framework, the letter 'I' stands for _____, which describes how hard an athlete trains.
Match each SPOR principle to its description.
right: Training load must be gradually increased to continue causing adaptation
Training must match the demands of the sport and the individual
Adequate rest must be planned so the body can repair and adapt between sessions

flashcard_questions.q: What does SPOR stand for in training principles?
What is the principle of specificity?
flashcard_questions.a: Training must match the specific demands of the sport and the individual.
Gradually increasing training load over time so the body continues to adapt.
Fitness gains are lost when training stops or is significantly reduced.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Recovery principle mean in training design?
flashcard_questions.a: Adequate rest must be planned so the body can repair and adapt between sessions.
How often a person trains per week.
How hard the training is, often expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the aerobic training zone as a percentage of maximum heart rate?
What is the anaerobic training zone as a percentage of maximum heart rate?
How are SPOR and FITT related?
flashcard_questions.a: SPOR gives the principles (why); FITT provides the variables to apply them (how).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does progressive overload require a gradual increase rather than a sudden one?
flashcard_questions.a: Too-rapid increases cause injury; gradual increases allow the body to adapt safely.

flashcard_questions.q: Which FITT variable must match the principle of specificity most closely?
flashcard_questions.a: Type — the training method must replicate the demands of the sport.

glossary_terms.definition: An acronym for the OCR training principles: Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility and Recovery.
An acronym describing the four training variables that can be manipulated to create progression: Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type.
Training must be matched to the specific demands of the sport or activity, targeting the relevant muscles, energy systems and movement patterns.
Training load must be gradually increased over time to continue creating overload on the body, as adaptations occur and the same stimulus no longer challenges the performer.
Fitness gains are lost when training stops or is significantly reduced; the rate of loss varies by component, but cardiovascular fitness declines faster than muscular strength.
Adequate rest and recovery time built into a training programme so the body can repair, adapt and improve between sessions.

hero_image_caption: Systematic training based on the SPOR and FITT principles drives measurable fitness gains.
